title: Predicting Dataset Influence Without Training
one_liner: A training-free metric predicts which datasets will help a multimodal language model learn a target task, before any training starts.
lead: Multimodal language models learn from huge datasets. When you want to teach one a new task, picking the right training dataset is hard: conventional wisdom says choose the dataset that looks most similar to your target, but this guess fails constantly because intuitive similarity does not predict actual transfer. DATAPROPHET ranks datasets before any training by measuring three observable quantities—model confusion (high confusion signals new patterns to learn), task overlap (shared structure accelerates transfer), and dataset diversity (variety prevents learning plateaus)—and the predicted ranking matches real training outcomes 86 percent of the time.

problem.h2: Picking the right training dataset is a guessing game
paras: Multimodal language models (models that understand both images and text together) learn from huge datasets. When you want to teach one a new task, you have to pick which dataset to train on. Right now, people guess: 'That dataset looks similar to my task, so it will probably work.' But this guess fails constantly.

A beginner might reason: 'Text-heavy datasets help text tasks, vision-heavy datasets help vision tasks.' Yet the paper's experiments on 14 real datasets show this intuition is backwards—transfer jumps around unpredictably because what matters is not the broad category but the precise overlap between the dataset's examples and the target task, plus how much the model can learn from the dataset's complexity and diversity. The specific dataset matters far more than the broad category. You end up wasting time training on the wrong dataset and only finding out after weeks of compute.

callout.html: You cannot predict in advance whether a dataset will help your model learn a new task; today's practice is to train on each candidate and measure performance after weeks of compute, so you waste time and money on bad choices because the training cost masks which dataset is truly useful.

steps.text: Measure how confused the model is by the dataset (perplexity), how close the dataset is to the target task, and how varied the dataset is.
Blend perplexity, similarity, and diversity into one ranking score for each dataset.
Order all candidates from highest to lowest predicted usefulness.
Train on the dataset ranked first, without ever training on any other candidate.
After training, the predicted rank matches the actual performance rank 86% of the time.

paras: The paper ranks datasets by a single score—a combination of three easy-to-measure numbers (model confusion, task similarity, internal diversity)—without training on any of them. Conventional practice trains on each candidate and compares real performance; DATAPROPHET does it once, upfront.

hidden.name: dataset influence on target performance
paras: Influence is how much a dataset will raise your model's accuracy on the target task after you train on it. You cannot measure influence without training, but DATAPROPHET estimates it by combining three observable numbers: multimodal perplexity (how surprised the model is by each dataset), similarity to the target task (how much the dataset overlaps with it), and diversity (how varied the dataset's examples are from each other).

The paper measures whether this pre-training estimate actually predicts the real influence. It does: across 14 datasets, the predicted ranking correlates 86% with the ranking based on actual training results—strong enough to make dataset selection reliable without training.

heat.caption: Darker means more predictive of final performance. Perplexity and similarity drive ranking most.

reads.html: Influence is how much better your model gets on the target task if it learns from this dataset first, because training your model on a dataset teaches it patterns that transfer to new tasks.

Multimodal perplexity (how well the model predicts the dataset), similarity to the target distribution, and dataset diversity (how spread out the examples are) together predict influence with 86% rank correlation.

mechanism.h2: Why three numbers together predict usefulness
paras: A dataset is useful if three things are true. First, the model should be somewhat confused by it (high perplexity), because confusion means the dataset teaches something new—if the model finds the dataset trivial (low perplexity), it learns nothing. Second, the dataset should overlap with the target task, because examples that share structure with your goal will transfer knowledge more reliably. Third, the dataset should be diverse (examples should not all look identical), because repetition teaches less than variety.

The magic is that these three numbers can be computed in seconds—you feed each dataset into the model once and measure confusion, check the overlap with your target without any training, and check example diversity by looking at the raw data. You never train on the dataset. Yet the ranking you get predicts the ranking you would have gotten after training with 86% accuracy. That is strong enough to make the right choice upfront.

math.words: Predicted usefulness = a measure of perplexity + a measure of similarity + a measure of diversity
math.equation: score_D = w1 * perplexity(D) + w2 * similarity(D, target) + w3 * diversity(D)
symbols: the usefulness score for dataset D
how confused the model is by dataset D (higher = more to learn)
how much dataset D overlaps with the target task (higher = more transferable)
how varied dataset D is (higher = more examples to learn from)
weights that balance the three components

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Dataset A: perplexity 8.2, similarity 0.7, diversity 0.6. Score = 1.0 * 8.2 + 2.0 * 0.7 + 1.5 * 0.6 = 8.2 + 1.4 + 0.9 = 10.5
Dataset B: perplexity 3.1, similarity 0.5, diversity 0.8. Score = 1.0 * 3.1 + 2.0 * 0.5 + 1.5 * 0.8 = 3.1 + 1.0 + 1.2 = 5.3
Dataset A scores higher, so we predict A will help the model more. After training, A does indeed reach higher accuracy on the target task.

math.note: The three components measure different reasons a dataset helps: it teaches new patterns (because confusion signals patterns the model has not yet learned), it overlaps with your goal (because shared structure accelerates learning), and it offers variety (because repetition plateaus quickly).

charts.title: Naive: pick by task similarity alone
charts.note: Similarity alone fails because a similar-looking dataset may confuse the model or lack diversity.

charts.title: DATAPROPHET: all three components
charts.note: Combining all three metrics predicts actual performance with 86% rank correlation before any training.

items.html: A dataset can confuse the model yet teach nothing useful if it is too far from the target. High perplexity without high similarity leads you astray.
If all examples in a similar dataset are nearly identical, the model learns only one thing repeatedly. Diversity matters as much as overlap.
If a candidate dataset is so different from anything the model has seen that perplexity is unreliable, the metric may not transfer.
The metric assumes datasets are reasonably clean and representative of their domain. Datasets with mislabeled examples or extreme noise can corrupt the scores.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a sandbox with 5 to 8 candidate datasets for a real task (e.g., visual question answering or scene understanding). Compute the three scores for each dataset. Rank them. Then train the model on each dataset in turn and measure accuracy on the target task. Plot predicted rank versus actual rank and verify they correlate.
demo.closing: The demo must show that the predicted ranking matches the actual ranking at least 80% of the time, saving weeks of compute.
